01

What the project must solve

Goals and supported use

  • Review each test state once, with browser, theme, contrast, viewport, and framework variants grouped inside it.
  • Make changed pixels easy to inspect. Show original images without changing their pixels.
  • Make review fast and clear with the keyboard in Chrome Desktop. Keep semantic controls; broader browser, mobile, and screen-reader certification is deferred at launch (D53).
  • Connect a review to the exact commit and capture attempt that produced it.
  • Keep trusted reference images when older runs expire.

First-release boundaries

  • Ariakit is the first client. No billing, customer signup, or organization switcher.
  • Keep browser capture in the existing CI runner. No hosted browser farm.
  • Keep behavior and accessibility tests. A screenshot cannot prove focus order or a spoken label.
  • No AI verdicts, visual flake auto-approval, image editing, or comment system in the first release.
  • No changes to Ariakit source or public hosting in this design task.

User requirements pnpm, TypeScript, Better Auth, TanStack Start, Cloudflare, Oxc, Renovate, Changesets, Infisical, Lefthook, Vitest, Playwright, and a monorepo. Copy Ariakit UI components. Keep recipes and React components together when they belong together.

Current Ariakit evidence

Measured At commit 3ebb722, the repository contains 1,058 WebP reference images, 29,933,072 bytes (28.55 MiB). There are 372 Chrome, 372 Firefox, and 314 Safari captures. They sit in 26 screenshot directories. This is the current inventory, not a full cartesian product of every possible variant.

The capture helper expands viewports and styles, adds browser names, and uses test titles plus optional IDs and counters. Capture requires both CI=true and VISUAL_TEST=true. Keep capture in CI. Existing baselines provide workload evidence only; the first Ariviso batch starts fresh. Inspect the capture helper, browser setup, and visual CI script.

Capture constraints Current comparisons use threshold: 0 and maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.0005; full-page captures use zero allowed changed pixels. The visual matrix uses Ubuntu Chromium/Firefox and macOS WebKit. Preserve reduced motion, disabled animations, font readiness, stable clipping, and theme reload behavior. Current jobs retry failures with updated captures and replace the complete screenshot set only after all expected artifacts arrive for the latest branch tip. See capture CI and finalization.

02

A focused review workspace

The item list stays on the left. Its thumbnail always uses that item’s first declared variant. The selected variant never changes the thumbnail. The center holds the images. Review actions stay next to the result, with commit and run identity above them.

Working prototype · real Ariakit reference images, simulated changes
ariakit / ariakit · Example run · 3 items
Review required base 8a2f → head c41b
Accepted reference
Proposed screenshot
↑↓ items · ←→ variants · 1–6 direct selection · ⌘/Ctrl Z undo. F new only · Shift A/X whole item. Shortcuts work when this workspace has focus.

Demo controls explore behavior; they do not answer design questions. These images are copied from the existing Ariakit reference set. The proposed image is shifted by 4 pixels in memory. The red mask is a real pixel comparison of that simulated change, without antialias filtering. It does not prove production comparator behavior.

Information order: run identity, item name, full variant label, review state, image difference, then secondary metadata. Show “2 of 6 need review”, not just “changed”. Red marks always have a text count. An intentionally absent reference for an addition says “New image”; an unavailable expected reference says “Reference error”; a removed capture says “Removed”; a failed capture never looks like an unchanged image.

Incorporated A/X saves the current variant and moves to the next pending variant. Up/down restores each item’s remembered variant. F selects the full new image alone; it does not change browser fullscreen mode or select a different variant. S and D return to the two comparison views.

Settled whole-item shortcuts: Shift+A and Shift+X. Keep Cmd/Ctrl+A for Select All and Cmd/Ctrl+X for Cut. “Mod” means Cmd on macOS and Ctrl on Windows/Linux. Whole-item actions freeze the current sealed item’s added, changed, and removed variants, show their count, and save as one undoable command. During active review before promotion, they can replace prior verdicts, including automatic acceptance, on those variants; unchanged captures need no verdict. Automatically accepted additions and confirmed removals stay visible with “Accepted automatically” and do not count as pending. The next-pending shortcut skips them. After promotion, X cannot reject an automatically accepted variant (D24). For a human-approved variant, X can roll back the whole snapshot only while its promotion is current (D26). As an enforcement detail derived from D21 and D24, Shift+X uses the same rules for every target; if a target is protected, refuse the whole command and offer X on an eligible human-approved variant. Do not silently skip targets. A refused action keeps the selection. A saved rejection follows the normal next-pending rule (D03). Undo of your own saved approval follows D22.

Missing, added, and removed images

Engineering clarification: build the review list from the union of reference and candidate identities. Keep candidate order first, then append reference-only entries in reference order. A wholly removed item uses its first reference variant for its thumbnail. A partially retained item uses the first candidate variant. Do not use a missing file as evidence of removal. In F, a removal shows “Removed — no new image”. S shows the old image and an empty removed pane. D is unavailable when the old or new image is absent; keep the current view and explain why. D29 selects candidate order, then removed entries. D30 selects this absent-image behavior.

Viewer cases · D29/D30 selected behavior

Evidence must match the action target: on selection, clear or cover the previous pixels immediately. Show loading or an error for the selected comparison. Enable variant actions only when that comparison’s required evidence is ready. Whole-item actions still permit deliberate group review without opening every variant, but the displayed item and current comparison must be ready. Bind each saved command to the displayed comparison ID and revision. Failed image delivery offers Retry, never an unchanged result.

Keyboard and accessibility contract

InputProposed behavior
Up / downMove to the previous / next visible item. Stop at the ends. Restore that item’s last selected variant. On first visit, use its first variant. If a remembered key is absent, use the first variant and announce it.
Left / right; 1–6Move through declared variant order. Numbers select the first six positions. Arrow keys and visible controls reach all variants. Missing positions do nothing.
A / XApprove / reject the current variant. Ignore repeated keydown events. Show pending save and roll back on error. After a successful save, move to the next pending variant in visible order, wrapping once. If none remain, stay and announce “Review complete”. Rejection is reviewed but still fails the check.
Shift+A / Shift+XSettled whole-item shortcuts (D21). Change all changed variants in the current item as one command. Cmd/Ctrl+A and Cmd/Ctrl+X keep their native behavior.
S / D / FSelect side-by-side / pixel diff / full new image only. Preserve zoom and image coordinates when possible. A wipe slider and overlay can follow later if needed.
Cmd/Ctrl+ZUndo the last saved review command from this review session. Restore the original selection. Never undo another reviewer’s later action. Leave native text-field undo alone.
Tab / EscapeTab reaches the list, variants, viewer controls, and actions. Escape closes help or menus; it does not reject an image.

Do not install page-wide letter shortcuts. Ignore key events in text fields, editable content, menus, and dialogs. Provide a shortcut toggle and visible buttons. This follows the W3C character-key rule. Use Ariakit composites for bounded navigation; keep tab semantics for a tab list and grid semantics only if the final interaction is actually a grid. See the tabs pattern and keyboard guide.

On narrow screens, put the item list above the viewer. Stack the two images. Keep large tap targets and all actions visible. Preserve original image resolution for inspection; “fit” is a display scale, not a new stored reference. D53 selects Chrome Desktop and keyboard-only review at launch. Verify that scope before claiming support. Narrow layout remains a design behavior; other review browsers, mobile workflows, and screen-reader certification are deferred. This does not reduce the screenshot capture browser matrix.

Selected · D28 D03 already selects the next pending variant. This chooses what happens when earlier visible variants still need review. If none remain, stay and announce completion under either option.

03

Stable capture identity

A screenshot item describes one state, such as “dialog / success / open”. A variant describes the conditions that produced that state. Give them separate stable keys. Display names can change without creating new history. Framework is a variant dimension, so React and Solid share an item for the same state. New captures supply explicit keys; no legacy filename import is required.

Identity lab · proposed

Capture ownership is settled (D27). Ariakit prepares each page condition, then calls Ariviso once for that variant. The reporter groups captures with the same stable item key. The adapter still validates and stabilizes the prepared capture before upload. It does not change themes, reload pages, or iterate the variant matrix. D32 selects a page function with explicit variant metadata. D33 selects a versioned manifest with compatible optional additions.

Adapter ownership lab · D27/D32 settled, fields illustrative
// Selected ownership: Ariakit prepares each condition.
// Illustrative helpers; selected page-function shape.
await prepareDarkDialog(page);
await visual(page, {
  item: "dialog/success/open",
  name: "Success dialog",
  variant: { key: "react-chromium-dark", framework: "react",
    browser: "chromium", colorScheme: "dark" },
});

await prepareLightDialog(page);
await visual(page, {
  item: "dialog/success/open",
  name: "Success dialog",
  variant: { key: "react-chromium-light", framework: "react",
    browser: "chromium", colorScheme: "light" },
});
// Two calls, one item, two variants.
// Not selected: Ariviso owns iteration and awaits preparation.
await visual(page, {
  item: "dialog/success/open",
  variants: [darkVariant, lightVariant],
  prepare: async (variant) => {
    await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: variant.colorScheme });
    await page.reload();
    await waitForVisualReady(page);
  },
});

This adapter works with Playwright. D27 assigns theme, viewport, and page preparation to the Ariakit wrapper. That wrapper also owns cleanup and iteration order. A preparation failure fails the test attempt; the reporter cannot treat a missing required capture as success. Compared with the unselected callback API, this keeps loop and cleanup behavior in Ariakit. Revisit it only if several clients need shared orchestration. Store the browser version, OS image digest, font set, viewport, device scale, locale, time zone, animation policy, comparator version, and capture options in a capture profile. Keep the stable variant key separate from that profile. A browser upgrade must be visible as an environment change.

High contrast and forced colors are different inputs. A contrast preference requests stronger contrast. Forced colors can replace author colors with a system palette. Keep both fields. Do not silently treat a Safari/WebKit run as branded Safari or claim that emulation proves native Windows high-contrast behavior.

type Capture = {
  itemKey: string;
  variantKey: string;
  ordinal: number;             // Stable display order from the manifest
  dimensions: Record<string, string | number>;
  profileDigest: string;       // Capture environment and options
  imageDigest: string;         // Hash of the validated image bytes
  width: number;
  height: number;
  source: { file: string; titlePath: string[] };
};

Byte inspection All 1,058 current files contain lossless VP8L WebP data; 358 contain the same embedded sRGB ICC profile. Only 989 byte hashes are unique, a 2.5% saving within this one set. The largest decoded image is 1,248 × 1,650. The profile describes sRGB; validate its actual interpretation, not just its name. Ariakit requests WebP directly through Playwright 1.63. D42 accepts lossless WebP and PNG, preserves originals, and requires tests of decoded color and alpha. Unknown profiles fail clearly. This does not require a PNG conversion.

Selected compatibility promise (D33): a versioned manifest, deterministic ordering, explicit schema validation, and no identity changes on title edits. Unknown major schema versions fail with a clear error. Optional fields can be added within a major version. Changing a stable key creates a new item unless a future explicit rename feature is added. No legacy import or automatic name matching is part of launch. D33 records this compatibility choice.

04

One rule for every main capture

A complete main capture becomes the baseline when every change has valid acceptance. Eligible new items, new variants, and confirmed removals are approved automatically. Changes to existing images need valid review. Unchanged images need no approval. An earlier approval counts only when the full comparison is still the same.

This applies to merged PRs and direct main commits. Ariviso waits for the actual full main capture after merge, so it can detect drift. It accepts the complete snapshot together; it does not mix approved images from one pending main run into another baseline.

What “pre-approved” means here

Maintainer choice An eligible new item, new variant, or confirmed removal does not wait for a person to press A. The service records “Accepted automatically” after capture validation and comparison finish. The first complete main batch is also automatic. This does not permit incomplete runs, corrupt images, missing reference data, or existing visual changes to pass.

First acceptance within a verified lineage (D34): automatic acceptance applies to the first valid capture of a new item or a new variant in a sealed run. D23 includes variants added later to an existing item. Record its exact comparison tuple, policy version, and source run. A retry or merge can reuse that acceptance only if it is still exact and eligible. Example: a new PR item starts with no reference → blue and is accepted automatically. If main produces green, it needs review. Do not issue fresh automatic acceptance merely because the item still has no main baseline. Before baseline promotion, an explicit rejection wins. Undo restores the prior effective verdict, which can be automatic acceptance when undoing a rejection. Retries cannot recreate a revoked acceptance. Retain identity and acceptance metadata when image bytes expire. Independent PR lineages receive separate first-introduction records; D08 still verifies the actual merged comparison.

A key rename produces an addition and a removal. Both can be accepted automatically after full-plan validation; this is not identity-preserving rename support. D35 permits a restored key to reuse exact eligible earlier acceptance; otherwise it needs review. Missing reference bytes remain an error. The server derives these cases from trusted coverage and stored history; the PR cannot declare a required capture missing and call it removed.

Acceptance lab · service policy model, not live reviews

The controls explore the rule; they do not change a decision. The model assumes a valid sealed run except for missing-reference and missing-capture cases. Confirmed removals are automatic. Changed removal comparisons cannot reuse a different earlier acceptance and need review. A restoration can reuse exact eligible acceptance under D35; otherwise it needs review. Automatic acceptance adds no user command to Undo. This example stays before main promotion. After automatic promotion, D24 keeps the baseline and requires a correction in a new main capture.

Confirmed removals are accepted automatically

D59 selected Automatically accept confirmed item or variant removals after full-plan validation. Keep the Removed row and “Accepted automatically” label. D35 remains the separate rule for a key that later returns.

Confirmed removal: the complete trusted capture plan no longer contains a former item or variant, and all captures in that plan completed successfully. Missing capture: the plan still requires the variant, but its capture failed or never arrived. A missing capture fails the run under either D59 option. An image download or decode error is also an error, never a deletion.

What other tools document

There is no single deletion rule across these products. They distinguish the set of tests in a build from the approval and baseline rules applied to that build.

ToolDocumented behavior and limits
ChromaticStories omitted from the published Storybook are marked removed, and their baselines are lost. Partial testing should keep the full Storybook inventory and use test filters. These pages do not establish a separate manual-approval requirement for deletions. Removal behavior; partial testing.
PercyAuto-approved branches still pass when snapshots are missing. Its approval-required example reports a missing snapshot, then allows the build to pass once the present new snapshot is approved and existing snapshots have no differences. Partial builds suppress missing-snapshot notices and cannot become the full baseline. This is not a universal deletion-only approval rule. Baseline and approval rules.
ArgosDeclared subset builds ignore removals and cannot become baselines. Baseline builds must be complete, have passing tests, have no active rejection, and meet approval rules. Argos auto-approves its default baseline branch by default. These are build-level rules, not evidence that every removal everywhere is accepted automatically. Subset builds; baseline eligibility.

Capture failures are a different condition. For example, Percy reports no snapshots, unfinished parallel builds, and upload or render failures as errors. Percy failure types.

Selected tradeoff: automatic confirmed removals avoid a separate visual approval for coverage removed in code. Manual approval remains the unselected alternative when an extra coverage check is desired. This follows Ariviso’s automatic-addition policy; it is not an industry requirement.

Acceptance of removals

Selected · D59 A complete trusted run automatically accepts a confirmed item or variant removal. Missing, failed, corrupt, or unavailable required captures remain errors. Keep a visible removal row, exact acceptance history, and the existing rejection and reuse guards. D24 protects automatically promoted removals; D35 controls a later restoration.

D59 scenario · design model, not production evidence

Scenario: The baseline has button/light and button/dark. Case A: the new full trusted plan contains only button/light, and every planned capture succeeds. Case B: the plan still requires both variants, but button/dark never arrives.

The preview starts with the incorporated answer. Other choices show alternatives; only the decision controls below record feedback. No preview marks production evidence passed.

D59 covers removal of one variant and removal of a whole item. D35 still controls a later restoration. Neither option turns matching pixels alone into reusable acceptance, and neither changes when old image objects are deleted from storage. D59 extends D24 to automatic removals: historical X cannot undo their promotion. Correct through a new full main capture; a restored key uses D35 exact eligible reuse or needs review. No automatic service action enters the session Undo stack.

Removal acceptance uses the same validity guards: record the exact reference → absent tuple, policy, and source run after sealing and validation. Reuse it only while the source revision and lineage remain eligible. If a PR accepted blue → absent but main now compares red → absent, require review of that changed comparison; do not create a replacement automatic acceptance to bypass the earlier comparison. Before promotion, X overrides automatic acceptance; a retry cannot restore a rejected or revoked acceptance. Undo of that saved X can restore its prior verdict. D59 does not change object-retention rules.

Automatic removal correction · D59 with D24/D35

A complete main run has already removed button/dark through automatic acceptance. The new baseline has no button/dark capture.

This model assumes a complete valid main capture with no other pending changes. It illustrates correction, not service execution. A pending restoration requires a normal review; the existing human approval and Undo models apply there.

Is this the industry standard?

There is no single rule across these products. Initial setup, later additions, and branch-wide automatic approval are different policies. These documents were checked on 21 September 2026; they establish the stated cases, not behavior for every product version.

Product and casePublished behaviorEffect on this design
Chromatic: first project buildThe Playwright setup shows automatic acceptance of Build 1.Supports starting with an automatic initial baseline.
Chromatic: add a browserPreviously accepted Chrome stories are accepted automatically in a newly enabled browser.A precedent for automatic new variants, under specific conditions.
Percy: add a screenshot on a feature branchScenario 2 starts unreviewed and requires approval.Later additions are not universally pre-approved.
Argos: baseline branchBaseline builds on the configured branch are approved automatically.Broader than new-item acceptance. Ariviso still requires review for existing-image changes on main.

Chosen tradeoff: automatic new items and variants reduce setup work and avoid asking for a comparison with no prior image. They can establish an incorrect first image. Manual approval of every addition is the simpler alternative but adds work; it is not the maintainer’s selected policy. D23 applies automatic acceptance to new variants too. Display automatic acceptance separately from human approval so the source is clear.

// Proposed acceptance metadata; use the exact identity from D08.
type AcceptanceSource =
  | { kind: "maintainer"; reviewerId: string; commandId: string }
  | { kind: "automatic-new"; policyVersion: string; sourceRunId: string }
  | { kind: "automatic-removal"; policyVersion: string; sourceRunId: string };
// New item or variant, no reference → blue: automatically accepted.
// No reference → green later in that PR/main lineage: needs review.
// Confirmed blue → absent: automatically accepted.
// Changed reference red → absent: earlier blue → absent acceptance cannot carry.
// Before promotion, rejection wins; retrying cannot restore acceptance.
// After automatic promotion, keep the baseline and capture a correction.
Baseline lab · main changes and first-batch setup

This model represents one variant in a complete run. Production promotion waits for every required acceptance and all capture checks. D22 is settled: undo your approval only while its promotion is current. An automatically accepted first batch creates no session undo command; D24 covers later rejection.

InputSame rule
PR approved, identical comparisons on mainReuse exact approvals. The complete main snapshot becomes the baseline automatically.
PR approved, one image drifts on mainThe changed comparison needs explicit approval. Keep the previous baseline until every change in the main run is approved.
Commit made directly on mainUnapproved differences fail the Ariviso check. Approving them makes the full run eligible for baseline promotion.
No image differencesPromote the complete, valid main capture. There is nothing to approve.
Only confirmed removalsAccept the valid removals automatically. Promote only the complete actual main snapshot when all other results pass; missing required captures and changed earlier comparisons still fail.
First batchCompare against an empty reference. Every capture is new. The service accepts valid new items automatically and promotes the first complete main batch. There is no manual approval step.

“Same comparison” is stricter than “same new image”. Suppose a PR approved gray → blue. Main then accepted gray → red. After merge, red → blue is a different comparison and needs approval under D08. If main already has blue, the capture is unchanged and needs no approval.

type ApprovalIdentity = {
  projectId: string;
  itemKey: string;
  variantKey: string;
  referenceDigest: string | null; // null means no old image
  candidateDigest: string | null; // null means removal
  referenceProfileDigest: string | null;
  candidateProfileDigest: string | null;
  comparisonPolicyDigest: string;
};
// Snapshot IDs and commit SHAs are separate provenance.
// An unrelated item change must not invalidate this exact approval.

Pin the reference, then compare: reserve the accepted eligible ancestor snapshot before the comparison is created. Do not change a visible comparison in place. When main advances, the service can compare stored captures against the newer accepted reference in a new comparison revision. Carry only exact valid approvals. Recomparison of old PR images does not test new code combined with the latest target; merge validation still requires the current merge result or merge-group capture.

Promotion must move forward: atomically verify the accepted baseline revision and main ancestry when promoting. A delayed older run cannot replace a newer accepted snapshot. D36 selects this rule: a later full main run can pass an earlier pending run only if its full comparison includes and resolves all inherited changes. If the baseline advances first, make a new comparison revision and check approvals again.

Approval reuse also requires eligible provenance: this run’s review, or the verified source PR/run lineage for the tested merge and its retries. An unrelated, unmerged PR cannot approve a main change merely because its pixels match. Use verified GitHub metadata for source head, target head, actual tested SHA, and merge-group identity. Publish the result on the tested SHA. See merge-group events. Outside initial setup, an unavailable eligible ancestor is an error; it must not silently turn the project into a fresh baseline.

Acceptance remains valid only while its source is valid

Derived from D08, D22, and D26: a reused acceptance references the source decision and its revision; it is not a detached copied verdict. Recheck that source before publishing success and before promotion. If the source decision is rejected, undone, or replaced before promotion, invalidate affected active comparisons and GitHub checks. A later capture attempt alone does not revoke an acceptance already recorded; exact eligible retries can reuse it under D08. A promoted descendant needs the same current-promotion guard as D22 and D26: do not revoke an accepted baseline silently after a later promotion. Refuse a stale undo or rejection and offer recovery instead. A valid D26 rejection invalidates dependent active comparisons and checks just as D22 rollback does.

Atomic first introduction: record first automatic acceptance only after the run is valid, sealed, compared, and still the active eligible attempt. Reserve it atomically with the acceptance. This active-attempt check applies when creating automatic acceptance, not when reusing a valid recorded acceptance. An older worker cannot create first acceptance after a newer attempt superseded it. Once acceptance exists, a changed tuple needs review even if the newer run is still an addition. Use the existing acceptance and run records, not a new coordinator service.

Selected restoration rule (D35): a return may reuse earlier acceptance only when its absent → image comparison tuple, profiles, policy, source revision, and verified lineage remain eligible under D08. Removal does not itself revoke an otherwise eligible earlier acceptance. A rejection or Undo does. Matching the old pixels alone is insufficient. Otherwise require review; do not mint new first-introduction acceptance for a restored key. The legitimate current reference is absent; expired historical bytes are optional history, not an active-reference failure. Preserve identity/removal and acceptance metadata after byte expiry.

Tolerance consequence: under D07, the whole valid candidate snapshot becomes the next baseline. If the comparator treats a small difference as unchanged, those candidate bytes become the next reference too. Test successive tolerated changes explicitly; do not invent a separate hidden baseline rule.

Save, conflict, and undo

Ordinary review undo restores the prior verdict and original selection. A direct-main approval can also promote a baseline. D22 settles the boundary: allow an atomic rollback only while that promoted snapshot is still current. Historical snapshot bytes remain immutable, but the undone snapshot loses accepted-baseline eligibility. Revoke it as a reference candidate, invalidate active comparisons and checks that depend on it, and enqueue fresh comparisons. Keep the previous baseline’s bytes while this undo is available. If another promotion has occurred, ordinary undo makes no changes and offers a deliberate recovery flow. D22 and D26 are the settled rollback exceptions to normal forward-only promotion. Before promotion, a rejection takes priority over automatic acceptance. Undo restores the prior effective verdict; undoing a rejection can restore automatic acceptance. A retry cannot recreate a revoked acceptance. An automatic service decision creates no entry in the maintainer’s session undo stack.

Automatic promotion uses a new correction capture (D24/D59): keep the accepted snapshot, including automatically accepted removals. Historical X changes no acceptance, baseline, or GitHub result and creates no Undo command. Correct the code and capture a new complete main run. An existing-image change needs valid review. A restored identity can reuse exact eligible earlier acceptance under D35; otherwise it needs review. These rules still apply after a later promotion. D22 permits Undo of a saved human approval while its promotion is current, including a snapshot that also contains automatic additions or removals.

Automatic-baseline correction lab · D24 is settled

The selected model represents one changed variant in a complete main run. Production promotion waits for every required acceptance and all capture checks. The rollback preview preserves the unselected alternative for comparison. It is not the D24 contract. No real baseline changes.

Review commands on promoted history

D26 Any current maintainer can press X on a human-approved variant in the current promoted run. This saves a rejection and atomically restores the previous accepted snapshot. It works after reload and does not require the original reviewer’s Undo command. If a later promotion is current, refuse the command without changing any verdict or baseline. A on an already accepted historical variant is a no-op; it must not manufacture an undoable approval.

Three distinct operations: D22 undoes your own saved approval. D26 saves a new rejection of a human-approved variant and rolls back its current promotion. D24 keeps automatically accepted history and requires correction through a new main capture. In a mixed snapshot, rejecting a human-approved variant rolls back the complete snapshot, including automatic additions and removals, but does not revoke their automatic acceptance records. Targeting an automatically accepted variant remains protected by D24.

Derived command rules: bind rejection to the comparison, decision revision, promotion ID, and baseline revision. Commit the verdict, rollback, audit event, and pending check updates together. The rejection overrides the targeted main comparison’s effective approval; it does not reject unrelated comparisons merely because they reused the same original PR approval. Retain the rejected capture for review; revoke the rejected snapshot’s reference eligibility and recompare active runs that depend on that snapshot or changed decision. Do not accept a late success based on its old approval. Keep the previous snapshot’s bytes while D26 rollback is available, regardless of the 30-day closed-run window. A saved rejection remains until a new valid review command changes it; retrying capture cannot restore its approval.

Undo of this rejection: the existing review-session Undo contract still applies. Restore its prior verdict and promotion together only if the decision and baseline revisions still match the rejection’s result, the required bytes remain available, and all acceptance prerequisites still hold. If another review or promotion intervened, refuse without partial changes. Compare revisions, not only the current snapshot ID: moving away and back still invalidates a stale command. Restoring an older snapshot does not revive its old promotion command or an older rollback target. This is a new audited command, not deletion of the rejection record. A fresh A after rejection may make the complete run eligible again under D07; it does not bypass these validation rules.

Historical action lab · D26 settled

This model has one selected variant in a complete snapshot. Gray is the previous baseline; blue is the reviewed main capture; purple is a later accepted main capture. A real command must check every target and all dependencies in one transaction. No real reviews or snapshots change.

// A review command names an immutable comparison.
POST /v1/reviews
{
  commandId: "unique-client-command",
  comparisonId: "cmp_123",
  expectedRevision: 8,
  verdict: "approved"
}

// Proposed D26 command fields bind the current promotion too.
POST /v1/reviews
{
  commandId: "reject-current-blue",
  comparisonId: "cmp_123",
  expectedRevision: 9,
  verdict: "rejected",
  expectedPromotionId: "promotion_blue",
  expectedBaselineRevision: 12
}
// If blue is still current, reject and restore gray atomically.
// If another promotion won, return a conflict with no changes.

// Undo is a new audited command, not deletion of history.
POST /v1/review-commands/cmd_123/undo
{ expectedRevision: 9 }

Use an atomic, revision-checked database command. D1 supports atomic batches, but a conditional update that affects zero rows does not fail the batch. Guard the decision, audit entry, and status-update outbox together in SQL; prove stale-command behavior before choosing an ORM helper. See D1 batch and session semantics. A stale write returns a conflict and the current state. The interface shows who changed it. Retry of the same command returns the same result. Publish GitHub status from an outbox that reads the current run, attempt, and comparison revision before each write. Serialize updates per external check and reconcile after ambiguous failures. A delayed success must never overwrite a newer rejection, undo, or superseding run. Whole-item actions freeze their target comparison IDs and commit as one command. Undo restores the previous verdicts only if those targets still have the revisions written by that command. If another reviewer has changed any target, reject the whole undo and explain the conflict.

Do not claim a decision is saved until the server confirms it. Disable conflicting actions while a command is pending or serialize them. On disconnect, keep a visible unsaved state; never silently replay an old approval against a new comparison. D31 limits Undo to commands from the current review session. A reload clears that local stack. The audit log survives reloads even if the shortcut’s local stack does not.

05

Capture, import, compare, review

Capture CIPlaywright + write-only private upload
→
Trusted ingest serviceVerify source, validate images
→
Cloudflare servicesR2 · D1 · Queue → comparison Worker · review UI

Selected capture and upload path · D40/D41: keep capture in GitHub Actions. Upload manifests and image bytes directly into private Ariviso quarantine using a write-only capability. The service verifies a short-lived GitHub OIDC claim bound to expected repository IDs, workflow, ref, run, attempt, issuer, audience, and expiry. The capability permits bounded uploads and shard finalization; it cannot read private app data, approve, or promote. Public validated image URLs are readable without that capability. The service verifies actual workflow/run/attempt/tested SHA and the trusted capture plan through GitHub. A signature proves job identity, not screenshot truth. D40 selects GitHub OIDC; D41 selects bounded uploads through the Worker. Scoped stored credentials and encrypted artifact transport remain alternatives. Fork capture remains out of scope.

Public images and private transport metadata have different boundaries. D13 permits direct URLs for validated images. Manifests, review data, image-bearing traces, diagnostic images from failed test attempts, and quarantine stay private. D40 selects direct OIDC upload. A cleartext GitHub artifact containing that private data is still unsuitable; public repository readers can download artifacts. An encrypted artifact is a retained alternative. Public image permission alone does not authorize publishing the whole capture archive. See GitHub artifact access and OIDC claims.

The ingest service reads submitted files as data. It does not execute a PR script or install PR packages. Validate declared sizes, encodings, digests and decoded pixel limits. If archive transport is added, reject path traversal, unexpected entries, oversized expansion, and decompression bombs before decoding. Preserve the separation between untrusted capture content and trusted service comparison.

Run completeness lab · 3 required shards

Never treat “no files yet” as “no changes”. Seal a run only after every expected shard reports. The server checks counts, unique item/variant keys, byte hashes, image dimensions, allowed encodings, total bytes, and capture outcomes. A duplicate shard with the same digest is harmless. A different payload under the same shard key is a conflict. A retry gets a new attempt, and old attempts cannot overwrite it. A partial run cannot approve removals or pass the check. A sealed run remains in “comparing” until all required service results commit; only then can review begin.

// Proposed internal protocol, all calls authenticated and scoped.
POST /v1/runs                  // Reserve immutable run + shard plan
POST /v1/runs/:id/shards/:key   // Declare manifest + required blob digests
PUT  /v1/uploads/:ticket       // Write bounded quarantine object
POST /v1/runs/:id/finalize     // Seal capture plan; enqueue comparison
POST /v1/runs/:id/comparisons  // Recompare stored images under server policy
GET  /v1/runs/:id              // State, progress, errors, review URL

Use a short-lived upload ticket bound to one run, object key, maximum bytes, and declared type. Upload into quarantine. Compute the hash from bytes on the trusted side; a submitted hash is not proof. Promote only validated images. D41 selects Worker-proxied bytes; presigned R2 uploads remain an alternative. Presigned URLs are an alternative for large uploads, but they are bearer credentials until expiry. Do not put them in logs or reuse them as permanent image links.

Where comparison runs

D11 Comparison runs independently in the service from launch. D45 selects Worker comparison first, with a tested Container fallback. Selected shape: a Cloudflare Queue sends one comparison task to a separate comparison Worker. That Worker reads validated originals from private R2, decodes and compares them, writes the mask/thumbnail outputs, and records the result in D1. A stored run can be compared again without running capture CI. Record the engine, codec, profile, and policy versions in each result. Trusted project configuration controls baseline selection, effective thresholds, and masks. A pull request manifest cannot relax its own gate. Treat policy and profile changes as explicit reviewable changes before they can turn a previously failing comparison green. Never accept a pull request’s own “unchanged” claim. Queue retries are part of launch. Repeated delivery of the same task must commit at most one result for its comparison revision. Use leases, bounded retries, and a dead-letter queue; a failed task leaves the run visibly incomplete. A reconciliation job re-enqueues missing work after a crash between sealing D1 state and sending queue messages. Queue messages contain object references, not image bytes. Browser Rendering is not needed.

Selected runtime and format contract, still to validate: process one image pair per queue task in a separate Worker with pinned codecs and comparator. D42 accepts lossless WebP and PNG originals. Preserve their exact bytes. Compare supported static, 8-bit sRGB RGBA pixels under a tested color rule. Test the embedded sRGB profile used by Ariakit and unprofiled inputs; reject unknown profiles, animation, lossy WebP, invalid files, and unsupported depth clearly. Version any normalization. Lossless describes codec fidelity; two valid encoders can still produce different bytes. Playwright supports lossless WebP captures directly.

jSquash’s Cloudflare example shows explicit PNG WebAssembly loading. Its decoder source strips 16-bit input, ignores checksums, and does not establish color-profile normalization. It is feasibility evidence, not an approved dependency. Validate PNG signature, chunk lengths and CRC, bit depth, animation, pixel count, and the supported color profile before decoding. See the PNG color specification.

A 1248 × 1650 pair plus a full RGBA mask needs about 23.6 MiB before codec copies. Workers provide 128 MB per isolate, shared by concurrent invocations. Queue-specific limits allow 30 seconds CPU by default, configurable to five minutes, and a 15-minute wall limit. Use the stricter Queue-specific documentation where general pricing wording differs. Keep concurrency bounded and measure peak memory. See Queue limits and Worker limits.

D45 selects a tested fallback if a Worker cannot meet codec, color, or memory requirements. Use a Cloudflare Container with a pinned native decoder behind the same queue contract. This remains independent service comparison. It adds Container and lifecycle costs; it does not return comparison to CI. See Container pricing. No codec runtime probe passed during research: a disposable package download was blocked by DNS. Current findings are source inspection and buffer-size arithmetic, not a performance result.

type CompareJob = {
  comparisonId: string;
  comparisonRevision: number;
  beforeObjectKey: string | null;
  afterObjectKey: string | null;
  engineVersion: string;
  policyDigest: string;
};
// Commit deterministic outputs once, then acknowledge the task.
// Recomparison creates a new revision; it does not alter an old verdict.
Service comparison lab · no CI rerun

Two retry levels, one authoritative capture plan

Full coverage is required for the merge check. A complete declared subset is not a complete full run. Only the full suite invocation and shard plan reserved by trusted project configuration can satisfy the required PR or merge-group check. The capture manifest’s own coverage: "full" is not proof. The trusted orchestration must establish the plan and validate completion. D37 accepts full runs only at launch; refuse intentionally partial uploads. D39 places the trusted plan in Ariakit main configuration. Informational subset support remains a later alternative.

Playwright test retries: the reporter records test ID, test retry index, workflow run ID, workflow attempt, and shard identity separately. D58 selects captures from the final successful test attempt before sealing. If a test captured blue, failed afterward, then captured green and passed, only green is eligible. Failed-attempt images are private diagnostic evidence. Exhausted retries or missing required captures prevent a passing run. This preserves Ariakit’s configured test retries; it does not treat visual flakiness as automatic approval.

Workflow reruns (D38): when only failed jobs rerun, inherit verified successful shards from jobs that were not rerun. Require the same tested SHA, trusted plan, and the same per-shard capture-profile identities. Preserve each inherited shard’s source attempt. A job explicitly rerun must supply its new successful result; a failed rerun cannot fall back to its old success. Missing or incompatible evidence leaves the new attempt incomplete and asks for a full rerun. New attempts cannot let late old uploads overwrite selected shards. See GitHub rerun behavior.

Keep screenshot stability when removing local assertions. Playwright’s screenshot assertion waits for consecutive captures with the same result. D44 selects an adapter that retains equivalent bounded stability behavior with the same effective capture options before upload. A timeout is a capture failure, including for a new item. Stable dimensions alone are insufficient. Pin and test the exact stability policy; it is separate from service comparison against the accepted baseline.

Capture and acceptance invariants · proposed protocol model

A behavior model only. These invariants still require reporter, database, and GitHub integration tests.

Full runs only (D37): the server accepts only the full trusted capture plan at launch. A caller cannot make a subset complete by changing its coverage label. Only a complete full run can infer removals or replace the full baseline. Accept eligible new items and variants automatically after validation and comparison. Existing-image changes still require valid review. D59 automatically accepts confirmed removals under the same validity and exact reuse guards. Any rejection, pending decision, capture failure, or stale comparison prevents a passing gate.

Diff alternatives: exact decoded-pixel comparison is easy to explain but catches rendering noise; pixel comparison with explicit antialias rules fits existing practice but needs a pinned engine; perceptual comparison can reduce noise but can hide small defects. D43 selects a defect/noise study before choosing the new comparison policy. Current Ariakit thresholds are a reference alternative, not the selected new default. Compare meaningful small defects and repeated clean captures; record false-positive and missed-defect results. Final thresholds remain unselected until the measured proposal is approved. The fresh first batch removes any requirement for legacy baseline import; comparator behavior must still be explicit and tested. Show changed pixel count, ratio, dimensions, engine, and threshold. Treat size changes as changes. Use lossless source bytes or a verified lossless encoding; a thumbnail never becomes a baseline.

Prior art and alternatives

ShapeStrengthCost, migration, and reason to revisit
CI capture + trusted CI comparison + review appSmallest service. Keeps the current image environment. Easy to inspect and roll back.Recomparison needs a trusted job. Test artifacts, exact engine parity, and delayed reviews. Minimal alternative, not selected (D11).
CI capture + central comparisonOne service can recompute stored images and retry independently.More decoding, queue, resource, and cleanup work. Selected for launch (D11). Validate the runtime and codecs before deployment; retain the worker-independent protocol.
Use Argos or ChromaticExisting image review and baseline operations. Less code to own.Less control over grouping and key behavior. Validate exact workflow fit and migration/export support before buying; no current-price claim is made here.
Cloud capture and reviewOne service owns the full run.Must reproduce Linux and macOS capture environments, dependencies, and secrets. Outside first-release scope.

Argos metadata keeps capture order and retry details explicit. Its parallel upload guide distinguishes count-based completion from finalization; a missing shard can leave count mode waiting. Its subset design avoids treating absent captures as removals. These support an explicit run plan.

Chromatic’s baseline model includes Git-history, squash, and rebase rules. This shows the cost of branch-aware inheritance. Ariviso’s proposed smaller rule uses immutable comparisons and exact approval reuse; it must be tested against parallel merges.

06

GitHub login and maintainer access

Better Auth establishes identity. A separate server check grants access. Store GitHub’s numeric user ID, not only a username. A renamed account must not gain or lose access by accident. Check current permission on protected app data and review mutations. Validated image bytes have a separate public route. Client-side route guards are not an authorization boundary.

Access policy lab · no real authentication

Use a GitHub App installation for repository permissions, verified webhooks, workflow verification, and Checks. Keep its installation token separate from each user’s Better Auth login token. Request only required permissions: repository metadata, actions read, checks write, pull requests read, plus Contents read if needed for ancestry and organization members read only if team membership is the chosen rule. The GitHub App sign-in path can also need account email-read permission for Better Auth. Confirm endpoint permissions during the integration spike.

Private review data, minimal public status

D25 The maintainer confirmed generic public status plus a sign-in review link. Public GitHub check results can be read without Ariviso login. Use a fixed allowlist for public check fields: check name, tested commit, generic running/pass/fail state, and the authenticated review URL. Do not include thumbnails, private item labels, reviewer identities, or per-image verdicts in check output, annotations, or logs. The review URL must check authorization before returning data. See public check-run access.

Privacy boundary lab · no real access

Recheck current permission for private app reads and all review writes, including Undo. A public image URL does not use the login cookie or D46 permission cache. D46 records a five-minute protected-image-read choice, now inactive after the public-image clarification; do not silently apply it to private app metadata. Permission errors produce a temporary service error and refuse protected access. New maintainer accounts can join through GitHub login; there is no password signup or independent invitation system.

Use secure, HTTP-only, same-site session cookies, fixed trusted origins, server-side validation, and CSRF protection from the framework/auth integration. Keep GitHub tokens encrypted when stored. Separate production, preview, and local secrets through Infisical. Preview deployments must not accept production sessions or access production image buckets. Keep an audit trail for sign-in, review, undo, baseline promotion, and administrative access changes.

D1 uses an adapter/dialect path that must be pinned and tested. These sources establish a supported route, not a tested Ariviso deployment: TanStack hosting, Cloudflare guide, Better Auth integration, database adapters.

Do not equate the permission string with a named GitHub role: the repository API maps maintain to legacy write, while role_name retains the role. Team checks include child teams. See repository permissions and team membership.

07

Cheap storage starts with ordinary R2

D47 selected; image privacy clarified Use a private R2 Standard bucket per environment and serve validated images from a public read-only Worker route. Start with per-run object keys and separate protected baseline snapshot prefixes. Keep verified digests and relationships in D1. D16 defers deduplication. Generate small thumbnails once and masks only for changed pairs. The calculator models object count and mean bytes separately; it gives no deduplication discount.

Incremental R2 Standard cost · USD/month · scenario, not a budget

Existing account R2 use: unknown. Zero below is an editable scenario, not an account reading.

Rates checked 21 September 2026: Standard storage is $0.015 / GB-month, Class A operations $4.50 / million, Class B operations $0.36 / million, and R2 egress is free. The monthly free allocation is 10 GB-month, one million Class A operations, and ten million Class B operations, shared across the account. See R2 pricing and billing-unit rounding.

The growth scenario uses 10,580 images per run and an editable 10 KB mean original. The count comes from the maintainer’s approximate 10× expectation; 10 KB is an illustration, not a measured forecast. The measured current mean is 28.29 KB across 1,058 images. Stored bytes and object operations are independent: smaller images reduce storage but not the number of uploads. By default, one derived-image write per original and 25% extra stored bytes illustrate thumbnail overhead. Set both to zero for originals only. Use measured values before approving a budget.

Monthly costs use 30 days, steady retention, per-run objects, decimal KB/GB, and R2 billing-unit rounding. Background account use defaults to zero as an explicit unknown-usage scenario. The estimate is bill(existing + project) − bill(existing), so it does not give this project a second free allocation. It excludes staging/baseline copies, LIST/HEAD and failed operations, pinned history, backups, partial-month effects, CPU, D1, and Queue charges. Public delivery may add Worker requests and R2 reads; cache behavior must be measured.

OptionWhy / why notWhen to revisit

Retention and review links are tied to CI artifacts, and grouped persistent approvals still need a service.Archives with private manifests or diagnostics do not meet D13. Direct private OIDC upload is selected; validated image URLs are public separately.

Public image bytes, private app: serve GET /images/:id through the existing Worker. Resolve the ID to a validated original, thumbnail, or diff image record. Do not accept arbitrary bucket keys or expose quarantine, manifests, diagnostics, listings, or review metadata. Return only the image with a strict content type and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Public image caching must stay separate from private app responses. This needs no per-maintainer R2 permissions. See R2 Worker bindings.

Anyone with an image URL can view and copy its pixels; opaque IDs are not access control. App-access revocation cannot recall those copies. D15 controls service retention, not copies held elsewhere. A dedicated public delivery bucket on a custom domain is a viable later alternative if measurements justify avoiding Worker requests; it adds validated-object copies and lifecycle work. Keep mixed quarantine/app storage private. Cloudflare documents public buckets and development-only r2.dev.

Retention must follow references

D15 settles a 30-day retention window for closed, unpinned runs. Keep active baselines, open reviews, and pinned runs regardless of age. Pin the previous accepted snapshot while a current human-approved promotion can be rolled back under D22 or D26. Pin all evidence needed by an available Undo command, including a saved post-promotion rejection. Release these pins only when no active comparison, review, or recovery command needs the bytes. For per-run storage, copy a fully validated baseline snapshot to a protected prefix before moving its database pointer. Delete expired run prefixes only after the promotion lease has ended. If deduplication is added later, first expire metadata references, then atomically mark an unreferenced blob as deleting. Block new references to that state, wait through a grace period, and delete. A last-minute reference check alone still has a race. Quarantine can have a simple short bucket lifecycle; accepted originals cannot expire only by object age.

Total platform cost and failure boundaries

Workers Paid is already active on this account. Ariviso adds no second $5 base subscription. The account plan includes 10 million requests and 30 million CPU milliseconds; only incremental usage and overages should be attributed here. Measure auth/server-rendering CPU and resource use on the selected Paid plan. D1 Paid includes 5 GB storage, 25 billion rows read, and 50 million rows written; indexes also add write work. Images stay outside SQL. These allowances may be shared with other account use. The selected comparison service also adds Queue operations: one million included monthly, then $0.40 per million. A small successful task normally uses three operations; retries and larger messages add more. The R2 calculator above excludes comparison CPU and Queue charges.

Cloudflare Images pricing is based on stored and delivered image counts and optional transforms. Its “variants” are transformed versions of one original; Ariviso variants are separate browser/theme captures. Avoid conflating the two.

R2 signed URLs work on the S3 API domain and remain reusable until expiry. R2 bindings support checksum validation and conditional writes. Same-key write limits mean concurrent dedup uploads need coordination. Lifecycle expiry is appropriate for quarantine, not live shared baseline blobs.

Queues deliver at least once; the launch comparison consumer needs repeat-safe commands. See delivery guarantees. Do not add Workflows only to model ordinary run state; its current step and storage charges also need a reason.

Compute limit to measure: a Worker isolate has 128 MB of memory. Three RGBA buffers for a 3840 × 2160 comparison use about 95 MiB before codec overhead. Current Ariakit images are smaller; the calculation is a risk example, not a measured failure. See Workers limits. This sets a measurement gate for the selected service runtime. Use bounded jobs, reject unsupported images clearly, and keep a Cloudflare Container as an alternative if the Worker cannot meet memory or codec needs.

Relevant platform report: workers-sdk #6411 describes conditional puts with Miniflare 3.20240725.0. It is closed as not planned; comments were unavailable in the accessible view. Verify the exact condition locally and remotely before depending on it.

Copy Ariakit UI with its dependency closure

The current Ariakit UI package is private. Copy components, recipes, CSS, and required utilities together, keeping attribution and the source commit. Rewrite local imports. Include the required Tailwind/Ariakit styling setup and Clava. A copied button file alone is not enough: it depends on control, layer, hover, focus, glider, and active recipes.

// apps/web/src/components/button.tsx
// The full recipe and its local dependencies are copied from Ariakit UI.
import * as ak from "@ariakit/react";
import { splitProps, type VariantProps } from "clava";

export const button = /* copied full Clava recipe */;

export interface ButtonProps
  extends ak.ButtonProps, VariantProps<typeof button> {}

export function Button(props: ButtonProps) {
  const [variants, rest] = splitProps(props, button);
  const disabled = props.disabled ||
    props["aria-disabled"] === true || props["aria-disabled"] === "true";
  return <ak.Button
    {...button.jsx({ ...variants, $disabled: variants.$disabled ?? disabled })}
    {...rest}
  />;
}

This excerpt shows the requested file contract. The recipe placeholder is intentional and is not runnable source. The current wrapper’s disabled-state handling is preserved in the example. Copy the complete recipe during implementation.

Data model and operational boundaries

Start with project, capture profile, run, shard, item, variant, blob, capture, comparison, review command, review event, and baseline snapshot records. A baseline snapshot maps stable item/variant keys to accepted captures; the branch points to one snapshot. Keep snapshots immutable and move the branch pointer with a revision check plus commit-ancestry validation. A late older run cannot move the pointer backwards; only an explicit valid D22 or D26 command can restore a prior snapshot. Unique constraints cover external run + attempt, shard identity, capture key per run, and command ID.

R2 and D1 do not share a transaction. Reserve upload state, write the object, then validate and link it. Failed links leave a reclaimable orphan; they must not create a visible accepted capture. Use reconciliation for interrupted imports. Exports include manifests, profiles, snapshots, review history, and original images. Database backups alone do not back up image data. D55 selects daily combined backup and a tested manual restore; drills must cover database records and image bytes.

09

Start fresh, then require the check

Rollout planner · proposed gates

D06 Do not import existing screenshot baselines or create a legacy path map. Add explicit item and variant keys, capture one full main batch, and treat every capture as new. After validation, automatic acceptance creates the first baseline from that complete main snapshot. The measured old set informs cost and test scenarios only.

When capture encoding or browser version changes, record the profile change explicitly. Do not silently reuse an approval under a changed profile. D20 controls when the new GitHub check becomes required. Removing old Git images is a later cutover step after the fresh baseline and service are usable; no history migration is required. Keep export/restore and rollback checks, including automatic-removal correction. Fork support is deferred; test collaborator PRs, main, and merge-group runs.

Two separate rules: acceptance and merging

1. Does this image need a person?

Eligible new items, new variants, and confirmed removals start with automatic acceptance. Existing-image changes and ineligible restored or drifted comparisons need review. Capture failures never pass.

2. Must GitHub wait for Ariviso?

Yes, from launch after setup checks. A PR containing only eligible additions or confirmed removals can pass automatically. A PR with an unapproved change cannot merge until it passes.

A GitHub check is a result shown on a commit or PR. A required check is one that GitHub must see passing before its branch rules allow a merge. Ariviso reports failure for changes that still need review or were rejected. Valid automatically accepted additions and removals can pass. D20 now selects a required check from launch after setup; the optional pilot remains an alternative in the example.

Merge rule lab · Ariviso is one of the repository’s checks

Confirmed rollout: establish the fresh first main batch through automatic acceptance and pass the readiness checks. Then require Ariviso immediately for supported PRs and merge groups. There is no optional pilot. Setup tests still cover capture failures, review, retries, main drift, undo, and merge queues. “Immediately” does not mean deploy an unverified service.

Approval updates the check. Capture/upload CI can finish successfully while the separate Ariviso check says “changes need approval”. The service changes that check from failure to success after review. It does not keep a GitHub Actions runner waiting and does not rewrite completed job history. For direct main pushes, the commit already exists; failure holds baseline promotion, not a merge that has already happened. See GitHub check updates and required checks from a specific GitHub App.

Revision 9 document verification

Passed 99 focused Chromium checks. Confirmed selected examples, automatic removals and restoration, keyboard review, rebranded package targets, saved-feedback upgrade, copying and portable export, tooltips, and 390/320 px layout. No uncaught page errors occurred. Wide and narrow layouts were visually inspected. These results cover the local design record only; production evidence E01–E08 remains Not run.

Rejected or deferred recommendations

  • Read-only human-approved history: not selected (D26). A current maintainer can reject a human-approved variant and roll back its current promotion. Later promotions and automatic acceptance retain their protections.
  • Adapter-owned variant iteration: not selected (D27). Ariakit prepares each page and calls the adapter once per variant. Shared iteration can be considered later if it has a demonstrated client need.
  • Manual approval for each new variant: not selected (D23). Accept its first valid capture automatically; later changes still need review.
  • Roll back automatic promotion on historical rejection: not selected (D24). Keep the baseline and correct it in a new reviewed main capture. Undo of a saved maintainer approval remains governed by D22.
  • Overwrite main on A: reject. It lets an unmerged pull request change other reviews.
  • Secrets in fork capture jobs: reject. Captures run untrusted code.
  • Age-only deletion of accepted objects: reject. Old bytes may still be the active baseline.
  • Public access to app data or quarantine: reject. D13 explicitly permits validated image URLs. A mixed bucket remains private; the Worker exposes only eligible image records.
  • Hosted capture farm, billing, and AI verdicts: defer. No first-release need has been established. Durable Objects are not part of the proposed Worker comparison path; a Container fallback would use its required lifecycle support.
  • Legacy baseline import and CI-only comparison: not selected. Start with a new batch and compare independently in the service.
  • Adopt Argos or another existing service: viable lower-maintenance alternative. Revisit if owning identity, variants, keyboard review, and integration costs more than those benefits. The user’s stated project direction remains Ariviso.

10

What the final four-reviewer audit found

The 24 product choices were settled; the implementation contract was not complete. Four independent reviewers checked the review UI, baseline rules, service/security, and capture/release readiness. They found the gaps below. The audit preserves the original decisions. Revision 6 incorporates both remaining maintainer choices, D26 and D27. The 27 original panels are answered. Revision 7 added D28–D58. Revision 8 merges the selected engineering plans, public image clarification, and WebP/PNG support. Remaining choices are listed at the top; E01–E08 remains unverified. This does not authorize product implementation.

FindingResolution in this designStill needed
Public artifact transport exposed private captures.Use private OIDC upload for manifests and quarantine. Revision 8 permits validated public image URLs; D25 still limits check output to generic status and a sign-in link.OIDC/upload capability integration and trace/report leakage test.
Complete subsets could be mistaken for full coverage; retry levels were conflated.Full trusted plan required. Select final successful test captures and inherit only verified successful non-rerun shards (D38/D58).Reporter and rerun fixtures; confirm trusted plan derivation.
Reused acceptance could outlive its source or race a newer attempt.Source-revision dependencies, active-attempt commit checks, and removal eligibility boundaries.Atomic SQL tests and delayed worker/check tests.
Viewer could show old pixels while acting on a newly selected variant.Clear stale evidence; gate current actions on readiness; show error and Retry.Production image delivery and revision binding tests.
Removed captures lacked thumbnail/order/view rules.Union of identities; candidate order then removed entries. D is unavailable for additions/removals; S/F have explicit empty states.Real addition/removal fixtures and accessibility review.
Human-promoted history had no A/X policy.D26 now selects explicit rejection and rollback of the current human-approved promotion.Atomic rollback, retained bytes, dependent checks, mixed snapshots, and Undo tests.
The variants array did not define who prepares each page.D27 now selects one prepared capture per call, with Ariakit owning page preparation.Public adapter types, grouping, ordering, and preparation-failure tests.
Removing screenshot assertions could remove pixel stabilization.Preserve bounded consecutive-capture stability before upload.Changing-pixels/stable-dimensions fixture.

Known work remains: codec and memory measurements, comparator parity, Better Auth/D1 deployment checks, public package names and supported versions, CLI commands/exit behavior, clean package installs, backup/restore, and launch review tests in Chrome Desktop. Broader assistive-technology certification is deferred by D53. These validation tasks remain unverified; the review does not count them as new discoveries. Restoration, scheduling, workflow reruns, API shape, and all 61 decision panels now have explicit answers. Revision 9 selects Ariviso, a single bare CLI package, automatic confirmed removals, and Chrome Desktop keyboard review. Measured comparator thresholds and numeric budgets must return for approval after evidence exists. Routine internal code details must satisfy the selected contract and its evidence tests; they are not additional hidden maintainer choices.
